title: Best Real-Time AI Sales Assistants in 2026, by Use Case
summary: The best real-time AI sales assistants in 2026, compared by use case: cold calling at volume, discovery and demo calls, and platform-native options.
body_markdown:
The best real-time AI sales assistant for your team depends on one question: which calls are you trying to win? This guide compares the established real-time assistants of 2026 by use case, from cold calling at volume to discovery and demo calls, with honest notes on where each one falls short.


## 01


What counts as a real-time AI sales assistant?


A real-time AI sales assistant listens to a live sales call and puts help on the rep's screen while the conversation is still happening: answers to hard questions, counters to objections, and prompts for what to ask next. That is the whole category test. If a tool records the call and gives you analysis afterwards, it is a conversation intelligence tool, and it belongs in a different comparison.


This distinction matters because the two categories get mixed together in almost every listicle. Gong, Fathom, Otter, and Granola are useful products, but they help you review calls, not win the one you are on. If a rep freezes when a prospect asks about your security model, a summary delivered an hour later does not help. For a fuller breakdown of the category, see[what a real-time sales assistant actually does](https://www.caretta.so/blog/what-is-a-real-time-sales-assistant) .

## 03


Best for discovery and demo calls: Caretta


Discovery and demo calls are where the hardest questions land: security, pricing edge cases, integration details, competitor comparisons. The reason reps struggle is rarely effort. The answers exist somewhere in the organisation, spread across docs, the CRM, past calls, and the heads of a few senior people.


Caretta builds a knowledge layer from those sources and uses it live. When a prospect asks a hard question or raises an objection, the answer appears on the rep's screen while the prospect is still talking, drawn from how the company's best reps have handled it before. It works before the call (briefs), during it (live answers), and after it (notes and follow-ups). The honest caveat: it is a young product, and it is designed for scheduled meetings rather than high-volume outbound dialling. See[the product page](https://www.caretta.so/product) for how it fits a full call cycle.


## 04


Best for cold calling at volume: Nooks


Cold calling is a different problem. Calls are short, most numbers do not connect, and the skill is handling the first thirty seconds. Nooks is built for exactly this: it is an AI dialler that lets SDRs work through call lists in parallel, with assistance around the moments that matter on a connect. If your team lives in a dialler and measures conversations per hour, start here. If your revenue comes from scheduled demos with committees, a dialler-first tool solves the wrong problem.


## 05


Best if you already run Outreach: Kaia


Kaia is Outreach's meeting assistant. It joins meetings booked through Outreach, transcribes live, and shows content cards when configured topics come up. Its strength and its limit are the same fact: it is a feature of the Outreach platform. For teams already paying for Outreach sales engagement, Kaia is the lowest-friction way to get live assistance. Nobody should adopt Outreach just to get it.


## 06


Best for battlecard coaching: Clari Copilot


Clari Copilot (which absorbed the earlier product Wingman) triggers battlecards when a keyword comes up on a call: a competitor's name, a pricing phrase, a known objection. This works well when the plays are known and stable, and when a sales enablement owner keeps the cards current. The weakness is structural. Keyword triggers only cover the questions someone predicted, and stale cards quietly train reps to ignore the tool. Budget maintenance time or skip it.


## 07


Best for phone-first teams: Dialpad Ai


Dialpad's assistant lives inside its own phone system and contact centre products. It transcribes live and surfaces assist cards for agents on calls. For teams whose selling happens on the phone system anyway, or where sales sits next to support, it is a natural fit. The trade-off is the platform boundary: you are buying a phone system with AI, and the assistant does not follow you into meetings held elsewhere.


## 08


What real-time assistants will not fix


A live assistant amplifies what your organisation already knows. It will not fix a broken ICP, a product that does not fit the market, or a team that has never closed the deals you are asking it to help with. If your docs and CRM are empty, tools that learn from them have nothing to learn. And no assistant substitutes for a rep who listens; a screen full of prompts read aloud in a monotone loses deals faster than silence.


It is also fine to need none of these. A three-person founding team selling to people they know does not have a knowledge distribution problem yet.


## 09


How should you choose?


Start from your calendar, not from feature lists. Count last month's calls. If most were cold dials, you need dialler-native assistance. If most were scheduled discovery and demo calls, you need an assistant that knows your organisation's answers and can deliver them mid-conversation. If you already run Outreach or Dialpad end to end, try the assistant you already own before adding a new one, and check whether it actually answers your hardest questions or just transcribes them. Then pilot one tool with a handful of reps for a month and judge it on one number: how often a rep used what it showed them.
